#### Governing Dynamic Capabilities: Cryptographic Binding and Reproducibility Verification for AI Agent Tool Use

问题与 changed constraint：AI agents dynamically acquire tools, orchestrate sub-agents, and transact across organizational boundaries, yet no existing security layer verifies what an agent can do, whether it executed what it claims, or what happened in a multi-agent interaction. We trace this gap to the capability-context separation: inside a transformer, tool definitions and user context are indistinguishable tokens, but at the orchestration layer they have fundamentally different security semantics. Existing frameworks conflate the two, enabling silent capability escalation and leaving interactions without verifiable provenance. From this principle we derive three Agent Governance Requirements: capability integrity (G1), behavioral verifiability (G2), and interaction auditab

We extend X.509 v3 with a skills manifest hash—a SHA-256 commitment to the agent’s complete tool configuration. Any mismatch causes immediate certificate invalidation. Certificates are embedded within a trust propagation tree where human and organizational entities form the roots, and trust constraints (maximum credential tier, delegation depth, allowed tools, rate limits) propagate monotonically downward. No agent can exceed the trust boundaries set by its human principal. Reproducibility Commitments (§4) G2. Given that the capability envelope is fixed (certificate-bound), we leverage LLM inference near-determinism [1, 6] to enable post-hoc replay verification. #### D-MEM: Dopamine-Gated Agentic Memory via Reward Prediction Error Routing

问题与 changed constraint：Autonomous LLM agents require structured long-term memory, yet current "append-and-evolve" systems like A-MEM face O(N^2) write-latency and excessive token costs.
